source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood, Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design
finding: Largest controlled test of analogical distance in design. Far-field patent examples gave more novel ideas than near-field examples, but not more than no examples.
numbers: 153 senior engineering students, 9 conditions (distance x commonness x modality) plus control; energy-harvesting problem. Distance main effect: solution transfer eta2=0.08, d=0.60 (far>near); mean novelty p<.05 d=0.56; max novelty d=0.56. Far vs control: no significant difference on novelty.
limits: Students, one problem, patent examples only; examples shown after a first unaided phase. Effects on mean and max quality were null.
agent_relevance: Far sources help novelty only relative to near sources. A retrieval policy for O7 should not assume far always beats no example.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood, Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design
finding: Commonness of the example mattered more than distance for search breadth. More-common examples narrowed search and cut output.
numbers: Commonness main effects: quantity eta2=0.12 (more-common fewer ideas, d=-0.67 vs less-common, d=-0.76 vs control); breadth eta2=0.07 (more-common narrower than control d=-1.03); mean novelty eta2=0.10, d=0.61 for less-common over more-common; variability in quality d=0.62 to 0.68.
limits: Less-common vs control gave no reliable novelty gain by itself. Commonness was a database proxy, not measured from each participant's memory.
agent_relevance: Familiar analogues fixate. A retrieval step should down-weight analogues the model already produces by default.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood, Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design
finding: Only the combination far-field plus less-common beat the no-example control on novelty. Neither factor alone did.
numbers: Dunnett post hoc vs control: far+less-common mean novelty d=1.14, max novelty d=1.29. Far-field alone and less-common alone did not differ from control (control sat in the middle).
limits: Cell sizes about 13-17 per condition (Table 1). Post hoc over four collapsed cells.
agent_relevance: Best retrieval target is far in domain and rare in use. Needs two filters, not one.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood, Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design
finding: Text examples were used more than pictures, but modality did not change novelty. The idea that pictures carry surface detail that blocks far retrieval was not supported on novelty.
numbers: Modality main effect on solution transfer eta2=0.09, d=0.60 (text>picture). No modality effects on novelty; effects of distance and commonness were not modulated by modality.
limits: The paper cites other work where sketches helped novices; not resolved here.
agent_relevance: Present analogues as abstract text; no evidence that richer detail raises novelty.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood, Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design
finding: Far-field examples had a cost: about one fewer idea in the fixed time. Mean and max quality did not change. Only the spread of quality grew.
numbers: Distance on quantity eta2=0.05, far vs near d=-0.30, p<.05; no distance effect on breadth (p=.78). Variability of quality: far greater than near (d=0.64) and than control (d=0.78), p<.05.
limits: Higher variance helps only if ideas are later filtered.
agent_relevance: Far analogues raise variance, not the mean. Pair them with a verifier and selection, per guardrail G3.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood, Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design
finding: Background section states the open disputes: far-field analogies are hard to retrieve or notice, and some authors dispute their role in famous inventions.
numbers: Cites: number of far analogies used correlates with originality rated by customers; surface-dissimilar examples raise novelty relative to none; surface-similar examples cut variety.
limits: Review claims only, taken from the paper's text; the underlying studies were not opened here.
agent_relevance: Frames the retrieval problem: the useful analogue is the one least likely to be retrieved by similarity.

source: Goucher-Lambert, Gyory, Kotovsky, Cagan (2020) Adaptive inspirational design stimuli
finding: Automatically chosen near or far stimuli (by LSA similarity to the designer's current design) did not raise novelty over no stimulus.
numbers: 66 participants recruited, 60 analysed, 20 per condition (near, far, control); stimulus mid-session after first 10 min; novelty change from midpoint to final design no different between conditions. Expert ICC for novelty 0.78.
limits: Only the two extremes, no middle 'sweet spot'. Small samples. Student designers, one problem.
agent_relevance: Adaptive retrieval keyed to the agent's current partial solution is feasible; benefit for novelty is not shown.

source: Goucher-Lambert, Gyory, Kotovsky, Cagan (2020) Adaptive inspirational design stimuli
finding: Near stimuli raised feasibility and far stimuli lowered usefulness. This is a measured cost of far analogies.
numbers: Near vs control feasibility change p=0.05, d=0.5. Far vs control usefulness decrease p<0.01, d=1.1. Perceived helpfulness near 3.5 vs far 3.0 (d=0.36, p<.13).
limits: Marginal p for the near effect. Perceived helpfulness did not differ, so designers could not tell which helped.
agent_relevance: Do not trust the model's own sense of which analogue helped. Check by code or a held-out test.

source: Goucher-Lambert, Gyory, Kotovsky, Cagan (2020) Adaptive inspirational design stimuli
finding: What mattered was the stimulus's own innovation score, not its distance. Distance only controlled how closely the final design converged on it.
numbers: Convergence (LSA cosine to stimulus): near 0.33, far 0.13, p<.01. Stimulus innovation score correlated with outcome innovation, rexp=0.67, CI [0.63, 0.70].
limits: Correlational on stimulus quality; the authors themselves say distance should be paired with innovation potential.
agent_relevance: Rank retrieved analogues by their own quality, then by distance. A good far analogue beats a bad one regardless of distance.

source: Fu, Chan, Cagan, Kotovsky, Schunn, Wood (2013) The meaning of near and far
finding: Reported (search snippet, and citations in Goucher-Lambert 2020) to define near and far by degree of surface match and to propose a 'sweet spot' between them. Full text not opened (link returned 404).
numbers: No numbers read. Goucher-Lambert 2020 cites it as the source of the sweet-spot idea.
limits: Unverified here. The sweet spot is a hypothesis about an inverted U; Goucher-Lambert did not test it.
agent_relevance: Treat 'middle distance is best' as unproven.

source: Hope, Chan, Kittur, Shahaf (2017) Accelerating innovation through analogy mining
finding: Learned purpose and mechanism representations retrieve human-judged analogies better than surface text methods, but only modestly.
numbers: Product pairs tagged by crowd workers. Precision at top 1%: purpose-only 0.739 vs TF-IDF 0.63, GloVe+TF-IDF 0.565, LSA 0.413, LDA 0.435; at top 25% about 0.478 vs 0.399 (TF-IDF). Recall at top 1% about 0.02.
limits: Negatives are implicit (non-selected results), so labels are noisy. Workers tagged some surface-similar pairs as analogies, which favours surface baselines.
agent_relevance: Separating what a thing is for from how it works is a concrete representation for O7.

source: Hope, Chan, Kittur, Shahaf (2017) Accelerating innovation through analogy mining
finding: Near-purpose, far-mechanism inspirations roughly doubled the rate of good ideas compared with surface-similarity retrieval or random inspiration.
numbers: 38 AMT workers, within-subject, 12 seeds, 749 ideas; 249 judged good (k=2 of 5 judges). Probability of a good idea, k=2: analogy 0.71 [0.48,0.87] vs TF-IDF 0.28 vs random 0.27 (B=-1.81, -1.88, p<.01). k=3: 0.56 vs 0.16 vs 0.14. Likelihood ratio chi2(3)=67.96 (k=2).
limits: Fleiss kappa 0.51. Only 9 seeds appeared in all three conditions in the main slice. The rubric (different mechanism, same purpose, feasible) itself rewards far mechanism.
agent_relevance: Strongest human result that retrieval by function and then diversifying by mechanism beats surface retrieval. The outcome measure is built to favour it.

source: Hope, Chan, Kittur, Shahaf (2017) Accelerating innovation through analogy mining
finding: The design copies a known timing finding: inspirations arrive after one minute of unaided ideation, then 12 inspirations for six minutes.
numbers: Phase 1 one minute unassisted; phase 2 six minutes with 12 inspirations over four pages; $1.5 per worker; 5 graduate-student judges.
limits: Timing was fixed, not varied, so the late-timing benefit is assumed, not tested.
agent_relevance: Show the analogue after the agent's own first attempt, not before (links to Einstellung and fixation subfields).

source: Hope, Tamari, Kang, Hershcovich, Cha, Shahaf, Kittur (2022) Scaling creative inspiration with fine-grained functional aspects of ideas
finding: Fine-grained purpose and mechanism spans improved search for alternative uses and design-space inspirations over strong embedding baselines.
numbers: Two user studies. Mean average precision 87% in alternative-use search; 62% of inspirations judged both useful and novel; relative gain 50-60% over best baselines.
limits: Authors' own data; product text, not engineering patents with verified function. Baselines chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: Supports structured function and mechanism indexing as the retrieval key.

source: Kang, Mysore, Huang, Chang, Prein, McCallum, Kittur, Olivetti (2022) Augmenting scientific creativity with retrieval across knowledge domains
finding: A flexible exploratory-search tool for cross-domain paper retrieval. The user evidence is qualitative: interviews with three scientists.
numbers: Three participants in the interview study; retrieval compared against TF-IDF and embedding baselines on selected seed papers.
limits: Very small user sample; no controlled creativity outcome.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. Use as a design idea (the user picks the aspect of the query), not as proof.

source: Sultan, Shahaf (2022) Life is a circus and we are the clowns: finding analogies between situations and processes
finding: A structure-mapping style algorithm maps entities between two procedural texts correctly in most cases and can find rare analogies in a large set.
numbers: Correct mappings 87% for procedural texts, 94% for cognitive-psychology stories; 79% precision at the top of a ranking where analogy prevalence is about 3%; robust to paraphrase.
limits: Needs a paired input; true analogies are only about 3% of pairs, so retrieval is a needle problem.
agent_relevance: Mapping a given pair is much easier than finding the right pair. Retrieval is the hard step.

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: story-level analogies from LLMs
finding: Picking the analogous story among four options is very hard for LLMs and embedding models, easy for humans.
numbers: 24K annotated story pairs. Multiple choice: humans 85.7%, random 25%, ChatGPT about 30%, davinci-003 37.1%, LLaMa-65B about 28.6%, FlanT5-xxl about 45%, prior retrieval method (Sultan and Shahaf) 44.9%. Analogies are about 3% of a categorised dataset.
limits: Options built with entity-similar hard negatives; models of 2023.
agent_relevance: Direct measure that LLM retrieval of structural analogues fails with surface-similar distractors.

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: story-level analogies from LLMs
finding: LLMs pick surface-similar hard negatives about as often as the true analogy. Sentence embeddings track literal similarity, not analogy.
numbers: Hard negatives chosen with similar or higher probability than the target. OpenAI-ada, SimCSE, RoBERTa correlate with entity and relation similarity but poorly with the analogy score. Fine-tuned FlanT5-xxl gives generation quality comparable to zero-shot ChatGPT; LLaMa generation +28.4% and +27.5% with the data.
limits: Zero-shot and few-shot prompting only; no reasoning-model run.
agent_relevance: A pure embedding retriever cannot find analogues; use relation-aware features or a structured index.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 matched or exceeded human averages on text analogy tasks without task training.
numbers: Tasks: digit matrices, letter-string (human N=57), four-term verbal analogies (N=57), SAT analogies (374 items; GPT-3 above the estimated high-school average). Preliminary GPT-4 stronger.
limits: Challenged on counterfactual variants (see b21, b22). Common relations are in training data.
agent_relevance: Mapping a given pair is not the retrieval problem; success here does not imply good retrieval.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: On story analogies, the one task needing causal relations across domains, humans beat GPT-3, and GPT-3 did not reach significance in the far condition.
numbers: Humans N=54: both conditions p<1e-22. GPT-3 combined p=0.0005, near p=0.0039, far p=0.065 (not significant); human advantage OR=0.37, p=0.0003, CI [0.21,0.63]; 15 of 54 humans chose the analogue every time. GPT-4 near-perfect near, better far.
limits: One small set (Gentner et al. materials, 18 source stories); GPT-4 result preliminary.
agent_relevance: Cross-domain matching is where the older models were weakest. Confirms distance as the boundary condition.

source: Lewis, Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: A failed generalisation of Webb 2023: on letter-string analogies with permuted or symbol alphabets, GPT models fall sharply while humans stay high.
numbers: Table 2 over all alphabets: 1,876 human samples and 6,840 per GPT model. Reported accuracies 0.753, 0.488, 0.350, 0.452, assigned to humans, GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 (row labels shifted in the text extraction, so assignment is inferred).
limits: Letter-string only; counting and indexing failures may explain it (see b22). Row-to-model assignment inferred.
agent_relevance: LLM analogy scores may rest on training-data familiarity. Test retrieval on novel domains, not textbook analogies.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Reply to the counterfactual critiques: the drop is partly a counting problem. GPT-4 with code execution matches humans on the shuffled-alphabet task.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and 97 (interval 2). GPT-4 worse than humans (P=8.9e-13); GPT-4 plus code execution on par (P=0.496). Interval-size effect not significant with code (P=0.066).
limits: Authors defending their own result; one task variant.
agent_relevance: Offloading indexing to code removes the failure. Fits our rule that the program counts and the model fills slots.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Asking the model to recall its own relevant examples before solving beats generic chain-of-thought on average and is about as good as hand-written few-shot.
numbers: Average accuracy gain +4% across GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces, BIG-Bench. text-davinci-003 GSM8K (table garbled in extraction): self-generated 61% vs retrieved 5-shot about 54% vs fixed 5-shot 50%. GPT-3.5 reaches 15% Codeforces Acc@1 vs GPT-4 baseline 16%.
limits: Smaller models (davinci-001, curie) did not beat retrieved exemplars (e.g. 9% vs 11%). Exemplars are same-domain, so near analogy, not cross-domain.
agent_relevance: Self-generated analogues work only at model scale and are near analogues. Do not expect bio-inspired far transfer from this prompt.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Generating knowledge before exemplars helps hard code problems more than exemplars alone.
numbers: Codeforces GPT-3.5-16k Acc@1: exemplars 11%, knowledge plus exemplars 15%; GPT-4 Acc@1 up to 19%, Acc@10 29% to 37%. Knowledge-first order beat exemplars-first (Table 7).
limits: One benchmark; contamination risk on Codeforces.
agent_relevance: Order matters: state the principle, then the analogue.

source: Bhavya, Xiong, Zhai (2022) Analogy generation by prompting large language models: a case study of InstructGPT
finding: Analogy generation quality rises steeply with model size; the largest model equals human-written analogies when it picks its own source.
numbers: Percent rated meaningful (3 raters each, 1,407 analogies). Target only: 1.90, 15.61, 48.29, 70.05 for 0.3B, 1.3B, 6.7B, 175B vs human 66.67. With given source: 8.97, 29.05, 38.46, 53.79 vs human 71.88. Fleiss kappa 0.347 (given source) and 0.553 (target only).
limits: Possible memorisation; kappa only fair to moderate; explaining a prescribed analogy is harder than free generation.
agent_relevance: Prescribed retrieval may hurt the large model: it does better choosing its own source.

source: Ding, Chan, Kittur, et al. (2023) Fluid transformers and creative analogies: exploring LLMs capacity for augmenting cross-domain analogical creativity
finding: GPT-3 produced cross-domain analogies that people found useful for reframing design problems; a quarter carried some risk.
numbers: 480 analogies over six design problems and three prompt styles. Median helpfulness 4 of 5; observable change to problem formulation in 80% of cases; one-shot judged potentially useful 80% vs few-shot 67%; up to 25% potentially harmful, 80% of those for upsetting content.
limits: Judged on usefulness for reframing, not on solution quality; prompt tuned iteratively; one model.
agent_relevance: Cheap generation of far analogies works for reframing. Needs filtering (25% risk, validity unchecked).

source: Ma, Grandi, McComb, Goucher-Lambert (2023) Conceptual design generation using large language models
finding: LLM-generated design solutions score higher on feasibility and usefulness but lower on novelty than crowdsourced ones.
numbers: 12 design problems; expert ratings of feasibility, novelty, usefulness; few-shot prompting makes outputs more like the crowd; adding the word diverse changed the spread. Exact means not extracted.
limits: Not an analogy study as such; measures the model's own idea quality.
agent_relevance: The model is a near-field generator by default. Far analogues have to be forced in from outside.

source: Wijesiriwardene et al. (2023) ANALOGICAL: a benchmark for long-text analogy evaluation in LLMs
finding: Embedding-space identification of analogies gets harder as the analogy gets more abstract.
numbers: 13 datasets over six levels (word, word vs sentence, syntactic, negation, entailment, metaphor); eight LLMs, three distance measures; difficulty grows up the taxonomy.
limits: Intrinsic vector-space test, not a task benchmark; exact scores not extracted.
agent_relevance: Similarity-based retrieval degrades where the analogy becomes structural or metaphorical.
